outline: Hook: Every autumn someone asks why Diwali has moved again; the story says the moon decides, and the story is really about living by two calendars at once.

In the USA, Diwali can fall a day apart from India because the lunar day is calculated for local time; check a panchangam set to your city.

faq.q: Why does the Diwali date change every year?
faq.a: Diwali follows the Hindu lunisolar calendar, not the Gregorian one. It is celebrated on Amavasya, the new moon, that closes Karthika in many northern calendars and Ashwin in the South and West. A lunar month is about twenty-nine and a half days, so the festival slides against the solar year, usually landing between mid-October and mid-November.

faq.q: Is Diwali on the same day in the USA and India?
faq.a: Often, but not always. A tithi, or lunar day, begins at a precise astronomical moment, and the evening when Amavasya prevails depends on local time. Because the US is many hours behind India, the Lakshmi puja evening can fall a day earlier or on the same calendar date. Local temples and city-specific panchangams give the correct evening.

faq.q: How do I find the correct Diwali date for my city in America?
faq.a: Use a panchangam, the traditional Hindu almanac, set to your city rather than to Delhi or Chennai. Many online panchangams let you choose a location. Your nearest Hindu temple will also publish its festival calendar. If the date and your work schedule clash, many families light lamps on the day and gather on the weekend.

takeaways: Sankalpam is the spoken statement of intention at the start of a puja, naming the person, their gotra, birth star, the time and place, and the purpose.
If you do not know your gotra, priests traditionally use Shiva gotra or Kashyapa gotra; not knowing does not block a puja.

faq.q: What is gotra and why is it asked for a puja?
faq.a: Gotra is a patrilineal lineage traced to an ancient rishi such as Bharadwaja, Kashyapa or Vasishtha. In a puja, it is spoken in the sankalpam to identify the family line for whom the ritual is offered. Many diaspora families have lost track of theirs. When the gotra is unknown, priests commonly use Shiva or Kashyapa gotra.

faq.q: What if I do not know my nakshatra or birth star?
faq.a: Your nakshatra, or birth star, is the lunar mansion the moon occupied when you were born, calculated from date, time and place of birth. An astrologer or an online panchangam can find it. If you truly cannot, the priest can perform the sankalpam with your name and gotra alone; the intention remains complete.

faq.q: What does the priest actually say in a sankalpam?
faq.a: A traditional sankalpam names the current cosmic era, the region, the Hindu year, month, fortnight, lunar day, weekday and star, then the devotee's name, gotra and nakshatra, and finally the purpose, such as health, harmony or removal of obstacles. It is formulaic on purpose: it sets one person's prayer precisely within time and place.

faq.q: What is prasad in Hinduism?
faq.a: Prasad, or prasadam, means grace. It is food, flowers, ash or other items that are first offered to the deity during worship and then returned to devotees. Before the offering it is called naivedyam; after, it becomes prasadam. Eating it is understood as receiving the deity's blessing, which is why it is handled with care.

faq.q: Why should you not refuse prasad?
faq.a: In Hindu tradition, refusing prasadam is seen as refusing the blessing and the relationship it represents, not just the food. If you cannot eat it for health or dietary reasons, the respectful practice is to accept it with the right hand, touch it to your forehead, and quietly give it to someone else or return it to nature later.

faq.q: What is the difference between prasad and naivedyam?
faq.a: Naivedyam is the food offered to the deity during puja, usually prepared with special cleanliness and not tasted beforehand. Once offered, it is considered accepted and blessed, and becomes prasadam, which is then distributed. The food is the same; its meaning changes through the act of offering, which is the heart of the idea.

faq.q: How does the Hindu calendar work?
faq.a: The Hindu calendar is lunisolar. Months follow the moon's cycle, divided into two fortnights, and each day is a tithi, a lunar day defined by the angle between sun and moon. faq.q: What is a panchangam?
faq.a: A panchangam is the traditional Hindu almanac. Its name means five limbs: tithi, the lunar day; vara, the weekday; nakshatra, the lunar mansion; yoga, a sun-moon combination; and karana, half a tithi. Families use it to find festival days, fasting days and auspicious times. Modern panchangams can be set to any city in the world.

faq.q: Why are Hindu festivals on different days in the USA and India?
faq.a: A tithi begins and ends at a precise astronomical moment, and festivals are often fixed by which tithi prevails at local sunrise, sunset or midnight. Because US cities are many hours behind India, that moment can fall on a different local day. That is why US temples publish their own calendars.

faq.a: Margazhi, running roughly from mid-December to mid-January, is said to be the pre-dawn hour of the gods, a year of human time equalling one day for them. faq.q: What is the difference between manifesting and sankalpa?
faq.a: Manifesting usually focuses on attracting a desired outcome by visualising and believing it. faq.q: What is sankalpa in yoga?

faq.q: Does manifesting work according to Hinduism?
